cases.reason: A JSON value that is not an object is not JSON-RPC, and is answered once with id null.
An array is not an object, so a JSON-RPC batch is refused whole rather than served item by item.
An object that is neither request, response nor notification.
A message with an id and no method is a response. Answering one with an error would be a reply to a reply.
A message with a method and no id gets no reply, known method or not.
A request id that is null, an object or a boolean cannot be echoed back as a request id.
The plain handshake opener is the only thing that makes a connection legacy.
A request that carries the modern version opens a modern connection.
The modern version on the opener wins over its method: the connection is modern and initialize is not a method there.
A refused opener still latches. Otherwise a client could fail a modern request and then move the connection to legacy.
An opener refused for its version has still decided the era.
Only a request decides the era: a notification before the opener changes nothing.
A legacy connection stays legacy: the modern version on a later request is ignored, and there is no discover.
A server that refuses the legacy era tells an opening initialize which version to use, and a second one is simply not a method.
data.requested is the empty string when the opener named no version.
discover lists only the version a request's _meta can name, with the cache fields and the server's identity.
The list carries resultType, the cache fields and serverInfo; cursor is ignored and no nextCursor is sent.
Every modern request is checked on its own: an earlier request's version does not carry over.
A version that is present but not a string is a malformed request, not an unsupported version.
clientCapabilities is required on every modern request, and must be an object.
The protocol's own example: -32022 with the supported versions and the one requested.
ping and logging/setLevel left the protocol in this revision; everything out of scope is an unknown method.
A legacy version the server serves is answered as asked.
An unknown version is answered with the newest legacy version, never with an error and never with 2026-07-28.
instructions appear in the handshake result when the server has them.
A handshake with no version is refused, the connection is legacy all the same, and no call is served before a handshake succeeds.
A legacy result carries no resultType, no _meta and no cache fields.
server/discover does not exist in the legacy era, and the layer declares no logging capability.
A modern call result is the handler's content inside the modern envelope.
The same call on a legacy connection differs only by the envelope.
An absent arguments member is the empty object, in both eras.
The layer does not enforce inputSchema: arguments that are not an object reach the handler as sent.
A missing name and an unknown tool are invalid params, in both eras.
The legacy era answers an unknown tool the same way.
A failure the handler declares is a result the model can read, with the handler's own message.
An undeclared failure must not leak its message: the fixture's holds a path under a home directory.
The fixed failure text is the same in the legacy era.
A cancelled call is not answered, and a request id is matched by JSON type as well as value.
Cancellation works the same way on a legacy connection.
A line that is not JSON is answered and the connection goes on.
A message is delivered when its newline arrives, however the bytes were split.
Two messages in one read are two messages.
A batch on the wire reaches §2 as an array.
A message with no newline before the input ends was never delivered whole.
The protocol's interim result: resultType input_required, the requests as a map, and the handler's state.
The retry is an ordinary new request: the answers and the state reach the handler exactly as the client sent them.
A result that carried no requestState is retried without one, and the layer must not demand it.
A server must not send an input request the client did not declare: the call fails as a tool error instead.
url mode needs the url capability; form support does not imply it.
An interim result must carry inputRequests or requestState; one that carries neither is a handler error, in both eras.
On a legacy connection the layer asks the client itself, with the old server-to-client request, and runs the handler again.
A JSON-RPC error from the client counts as the client cancelling the question.
A legacy client that declared no elicitation is never sent the request.

A tool set read per request is answered for that request's own client: listing may depend on what the client declared, and a tool left out of the list is still callable when the set returns it for a call.
On a legacy connection the client's facts are those of its initialize, for every later request.
A request digest is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the tool name and the arguments, so member order does not matter.
The sealed form, byte for byte: base64url of the canonical body, a dot, base64url of HMAC-SHA-256 over that body.
A state opens for the principal and the call it was sealed for, before it expires.
The lifetime is exclusive at its end: one millisecond before it, the state still opens.
At its expiry time exactly, the state is refused.
A state presented by another principal is a mismatch.
A state presented with a call it was not issued for is a mismatch: here one argument differs.
A body changed after sealing fails the MAC, whatever the change claims.
A state sealed under another key fails the MAC.
A string that is not two base64url parts is malformed, and is refused before any MAC is computed.
The checks run in order: a forged state that is also expired is reported as forged, so nothing in an unauthenticated body is ever acted on.
Expiry is checked before the binding.
